Saving the Franchise Model, for Good

Congress can end the flip-flopping on the ‘joint employer’ rule.

By

The franchise business model has a case of Washington whiplash. A decade ago the Obama Administration moved to broaden the meaning of “joint employer” under the National Labor Relations Act, so as to make McDonald’s, Burger King, and company potentially liable for the actions of local stores. The Trump Administration reversed. Then the Biden Administration reversed. A court blocked that. In a Monday oral argument, the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals sounded likely to undo the current standard.

This is madness, and bad for business and jobs. Congress can help by passing the American Franchise Act, a bill that’s as straightforward as it is short. “A franchisor may be considered a joint employer,” the legislation says, only if it “exercises substantial direct and immediate control” over local workers, such as on hiring, firing, wages, hours, and supervision. Writing that into law would provide certainty and end the flip-flopping at the Labor Department and the National Labor Relations Board.
